In the lead-up to Christmas, we wanted to gift ourselves a moment of calm, flavor, and beauty — so we headed to a festive afternoon tea ✨
This is not just a dessert set, but a true ritual where every detail feels thoughtfully curated 🤍

The tea experience @roamlic is presented as an elegant set combining refined desserts and delicate savory bites 🍰🥐
The table fills with light mousse cakes, beautifully layered pastries, mini baked goods, and sweets that reflect true pastry craftsmanship. Everything is subtle, well-balanced, and never overly sweet — exactly what you crave during the winter season ❄️✨

The tea itself is a highlight 🍵
Fragrant, deep, and perfectly paired with the desserts, it’s served hot and meant to be savored slowly. It’s not just about taste, but about the experience: unhurried moments, quiet conversations, and the joy of slowing down 🤍

The entire tea service is built around a feeling of warmth and celebration ✨
Soft lighting, elegant presentation, and a sense that you’re in a space created with genuine care and love for detail. This is not a place for a quick bite, but for truly living the moment 🌙🕯️

We enjoyed every bite and every sip 🤍
You can feel the respect for ingredients, flavor, and the guest experience. That’s why Anntremet offers some of the most delicious desserts in New York 🍰✨

If you’re looking to soak in a festive atmosphere, take a beautiful pause, and enjoy a refined tea experience — this is a place you shouldn’t miss 🎄✨

Annual release of the nama version of gokujo no kire. Nose of charcuterie, smoke, baijiu and melon. Smooth sweetness balanced with muted acidity and alcohol dryness, ending with a palette cleansing finish. 

I rarely get charcuterie notes from newly released Nama (this one was released from Shuzo in November 2025), and based on back label information it was made with extremely low temp fermentation. Curious where that smoked dried meat aroma is from - is it that 結の香- Iwate’s local rice used a lot by Akabu, when milled to 35%, has larger amounts of proteins compared to other rice varieties?

Around the table we also got some Alas de Pollo Seitan Wings, Yuca Fries, and the obligatory chips & guac. It was a killer meal before a killer night of music. I never imagined I’d be here after wrapping up a brutal eight-year journey to trial that ended abruptly. After bartending in music and sports venues, stepping back to observe humanity from a bird’s-eye view, after opening and closing a storefront with some incredible women and carrying that work into off-site events and workshops. Yet, here I am back in Center City, behind the bar, and on the edge of a bigger leap with @villagewhiskey .

I’m a firm believer everything happens for a reason and that timing is divine. I stumbled into this role and just knew I wanted to work during the day in Rittenhouse again. I can’t fully explain why, only that I felt called to it once the court proceedings were over. 

I think often of my days at @parcrittenhouse the stories, conversations, and moments that made the work feel enriching. That feeling is already back. The people I’ve been meeting have made me feel alive again.

My coworkers are an incredible team, and I’m deeply grateful to be here with you all. Sometimes you land somewhere and can’t explain why it feels right. This is one of those places, a beautiful pause before the next big leap in life ✨!!!

The last month and change contained a GREAT DEAL of events. Amongst them: a trip to Philly for the pure sake of seeing @wearedps at a music festival

I hate music festivals

But I desperately needed to hear "Lo Air," and at the time I bought the tickets, it was the last stop in Dead Poet Society's US tour and I was not about to wait for their next album/tour.

A week later, more dates near LA released. Ironic.

Whatever.

@loyalandjustin and I have already committed to the bit and booked [insanely cheap] flights and a hotel for Philly. (Lezzzz goooo!)

Anyhoots.

We did it.

A Friday redeye from LAX to PHL. No sleep. A morning at a local's diner, the farmer's market, several cups of coffee, several miles and miles and miles of walking, show at 12pm, and then we wait wait for DPS.

Babes. They played every song I wanted to hear, and MORE. The bassist was doing backflips. His strap slipped off mid-flip and he didn't miss a beat. Straight TALENT. I swear, the lead singer made eye contact with me (I was going off in the crowd. A girl can dream.)

Then another day of wandering around center city + hitting up the Barnes Foundation + an amazing 10/10 whiskey bar

In which: the bartender just moved from LA! And just so happens to know the company I work for! Of all the bars I could have walked into... serendipitous, unbelievable, I'm over-the-moon. 

A well worth trip. (Literally, hotel + flights + all food AND COCKTAILS came in under $500 for two days, three nights). 

All's to say: I want hand tattoos now. And I booked tickets for @wearedps's LA show in September.

She’s also enjoyed exploring the city through trying new restaurants, shooting photography, attending @philadelphiaeagles games and mainly attending concerts - about 20 a year! I even found the cutest little anklets for my right ankle (it’s always the right one for me 👣✨) and now I’m feeling like I need to go back for more!

South Philly has a rhythm of its own, and showing it off to my best friends always reminds me how special this city is. Stay tuned — we’ve got so many more stops to make and memories to create 💛

For the past five years, I've observed that even during the extreme cold, the East Coast has experienced a noticeable lack of precipitation. This absence of snow makes me feel less festive at this time of year and more concerned about the impact of global warming. We no longer enjoy whimsical moments like feeling a snowflake melt on your cheek while waiting for the bus stop for SEPTA, or snowball fights after school is cancelled. The extra time we used to gain for work, school, or other activities—thanks to snow days—helped us pause in our fast-paced lives, but now it is gone.
I wonder how those who grew up where snow was expected—and nearly guaranteed—feel as the year ends and another begins. It’s not so much that I miss the snow itself; I’m troubled that its absence highlights just how dry things have become, raising fears of fires reminiscent of Octavia Butler’s "Parable of the Sower." Before we can fully appreciate the season, it feels as if “’Tis the season to be worried” has become our new reality.

We no longer enjoy whimsical moments like feeling a snowflake melt on your cheek while waiting for the bus stop for SEPTA, or snowball fights after school is cancelled. The extra time we used to gain for work, school, or other activities—thanks to snow days—helped us pause in our fast-paced lives, but now it is gone.
I wonder how those who grew up where snow was expected—and nearly guaranteed—feel as the year ends and another begins. It’s not so much that I miss the snow itself; I’m troubled that its absence highlights just how dry things have become, raising fears of fires reminiscent of Octavia Butler’s "Parable of the Sower." Before we can fully appreciate the season, it feels as if “’Tis the season to be worried” has become our new reality.

Happy last day of #phillyrestaurantweek I didn’t indulge this year in RW like usual (I usually go 6-8x). Now I’m indifferent if restaurants will use this opportunity that attracted new customers to show off their craft and love of food  or will they optimize this time of increase volume to utilize their inventory and focus solely on the amount of business. I’m always curious is it quality or quantity, I find very few have a great balance. Anywho, I’ve been to seafood unlimited for restaurant week prior and it was INCREDIBLE (it was BYOB back then so you already have an advantage in my book). Although, this time was not as great as the last time, there were still some great menu highlights. The shrimp Mac & cheese was AMAZING! I was shocked at how creamy it was & the amount of shrimp. The seafood spring rolls also delightful. And any place with batter fries is a friend of mine. As established, I love a good cocktail, but these cocktails really lacked flavor, depth and the va va voom *You know that moment when you first sip a drink and time stands still and you savor the flavor and bless the bartenders hands* I so badly wanted that. Also the entrees we’re not as good as the appetizers. It’s like dating a man who in the beginning is great, sets the bar high and gives you his best. Then later the flaws appear and it goes downhill. I thought the steak was the best out of the three entrees, which is unfortunate because it’s a seafood restaurant. I liked the sea bass and the beans were delicious, but the fish def needed more seasoning, I think if you are going to pan fry a beautiful fish like seabass, there is little room for error. The shrimp fra diavolo needed complexity. It was shrimp, pasta and tomato sauce. It was such an abundance of tomato sauce it overshadowed anything else in the dish because it was so acidic. With that said, I am always willing to give the benefit of the doubt  when restaurants run specials because I know there is an influx of guest during a short two week period so the strain that puts on the kitchen is a lot. However based on this experience especially compared to the last I’d say it was 3.25 out of 5 ⭐️⭐️⭐️

For the past five years, I've observed that even during the extreme cold, the East Coast has experienced a noticeable lack of precipitation. This absence of snow makes me feel less festive at this time of year and more concerned about the impact of global warming. We no longer enjoy whimsical moments like feeling a snowflake melt on your cheek while waiting for the bus stop for SEPTA, or snowball fights after school is cancelled. The extra time we used to gain for work, school, or other activities—thanks to snow days—helped us pause in our fast-paced lives, but now it is gone.
I wonder how those who grew up where snow was expected—and nearly guaranteed—feel as the year ends and another begins. It’s not so much that I miss the snow itself; I’m troubled that its absence highlights just how dry things have become, raising fears of fires reminiscent of Octavia Butler’s "Parable of the Sower." Before we can fully appreciate the season, it feels as if “’Tis the season to be worried” has become our new reality.

Don’t believe everything you see, the food influencers are paid to promote and of course they are going to say everything is amazing.

The truth is, food was very mid, portions were small, and way overpriced for what it is. The scallops with the ponzu sauce was good but it was small for the price. Hash brown with uni did not work well at all. It was awkward to eat and the height made it impossible to bite. The hash brown was thick and hard as a rock. Everything just fell apart when you tried to bite it or cut in to it. The swordfish milanese was so thin and minimal it tasted essentially like you were eating breadcrumbs. Was it even swordfish, it could have been cod for who knows and it would still taste the same. The restaurant had good ingredients to work with but the execution of each dish is questionable. Even the cocktail was awful. Our server noticed I only took a sip and she kindly took it back without me asking. But whatever, we tried it and we would probably never try again. I love seafood but this was a very sad day.

For the past five years, I've observed that even during the extreme cold, the East Coast has experienced a noticeable lack of precipitation. This absence of snow makes me feel less festive at this time of year and more concerned about the impact of global warming. We no longer enjoy whimsical moments like feeling a snowflake melt on your cheek while waiting for the bus stop for SEPTA, or snowball fights after school is cancelled. The extra time we used to gain for work, school, or other activities—thanks to snow days—helped us pause in our fast-paced lives, but now it is gone.
I wonder how those who grew up where snow was expected—and nearly guaranteed—feel as the year ends and another begins. It’s not so much that I miss the snow itself; I’m troubled that its absence highlights just how dry things have become, raising fears of fires reminiscent of Octavia Butler’s "Parable of the Sower." Before we can fully appreciate the season, it feels as if “’Tis the season to be worried” has become our new reality.
